sources.title: World Models for Learning Dexterous Hand-Object Interactions from Human Videos

sectionsRead: C.4 Success Criteria for Simulation Tasks
C.5 Success Criteria for Real-World Grasping

Identity/version: the inspected title page identifies arXiv:2512.13644v2 [cs.RO], 16 March 2026. Its title and all nine authors match the catalog. The catalog records submission on 15 December 2025; this report reviews the supplied v2, not the original submission. No earlier version or revision comparison was supplied.

synopsis: DexWM learns an action-conditioned transition model in frozen visual features, using human hand motion to support dexterous robot planning. A hand-consistency objective preserves local finger information; CEM searches robot joint trajectories through the learned model. Simulation and small-scale physical grasping results support transfer after exploratory simulation fine-tuning, with substantial remaining placement failures and a strict distinction between predicted rollouts and executed actions.

problem.text: Coarse camera, wrist or text actions omit finger articulation, while large dexterous robot datasets are scarce. The paper asks whether egocentric human videos and non-dexterous robot data can teach a state-transition model precise enough for image-goal manipulation. Its dynamics include agent movement, object response and camera appearance.

contributions.text: A shared keypoint-displacement action space connects human hands, synthetic parallel-gripper keypoints and Allegro forward kinematics. A heatmap loss supplements global latent prediction.

Human pretraining plus exploratory robot adaptation enables planning for reaching, grasping and placing; the evidence supports this particular transfer pipeline, with image goals and embodiment-specific planning machinery.

inputs: RGB observation history; hand-keypoint displacements and camera-pose changes
For planning: start and goal images, robot kinematics and joint-angle candidates
outputs: Predicted future DINOv2 patch states and fingertip/wrist heatmaps
CEM-selected joint waypoints for a separate low-level controller; decoded images only for visualization

steps.name: Encode visual state
steps.detail: Frozen DINOv2-L maps 224 × 392 images to 448 patch vectors of dimension 1024. The default XL predictor has 456M parameters and 32 conditional transformer blocks.

steps.name: Align actions across embodiments
steps.detail: Express both hands’ 21 keypoints in the earlier camera frame before differencing; append camera translation and Euler-angle changes, giving 132 components. DROID uses concentric-circle dummy keypoints. Allegro duplicates its last finger for the human pinky; unused left-hand actions are zero.

steps.name: Regress future features
steps.detail: The deterministic CDiT-based predictor uses AdaLN action conditioning, initializes future tokens from the latest state and directly regresses features. Autoregressive reuse produces longer rollouts without diffusion denoising.

steps.name: Recover local hand geometry
steps.detail: A transformer head predicts 12 image heatmaps: ten fingertips and two wrists. Two-pixel Gaussian targets supervise this head and the predicted state. A separately trained image decoder serves visualization, not planning.

training.text: Pretraining uses 829 hours of EgoDex and about 100 hours of DROID; EgoDex retains its original approximately 1% test split. Adam trains for 40 epochs, batch 4096, with learning rate decreasing from 1e-4 to 1e-7. Context frames are sampled nonuniformly within four seconds.

Fine-tuning uses approximately four hours of exploratory RoboCasa data for 50 epochs, batch eight, learning rate 1e-5, including multistep prediction. The default collection perturbs Lift trajectories and randomizes objects to avoid successful grasps. Fully programmatic random targets yield 49% mean simulation success versus 53% for the default.

inference.text: CEM optimizes 23 robot joints through forward kinematics and latent rollouts. The objective combines terminal feature distance and heatmap-derived keypoint distance, weighted by 0.001, plus an orientation cost for grasping. Stationary-camera planning excludes camera-motion components.

Simulation uses horizon three, 512 candidates, ten elites and ten CEM iterations with receding-horizon feedback. Physical grasping uses horizon two and 256 candidates, retaining ten elites/iterations, and executes both waypoints open loop. Controllers interpolate joint targets. A teleoperated dummy grasp initializes the grasp-search mean.

equations.explanation: Equation (3): s denotes encoded observation states, a the intervening dexterous action, and f_theta the predictor with trainable parameters theta. The hatted state is predicted; during multistep rollout it becomes subsequent context.

Equations (4)–(5): P is the patch count, d feature dimension, p a patch index, and H,W image dimensions. V and its hatted counterpart are target and predicted hand heatmaps. The encoder remains frozen while these errors train the predictor and keypoint head.

results.setting: Franka Panda with Allegro; 12 trials using four objects; no real-world fine-tuning; two-step open-loop execution.
results.comparison: Diffusion Policy and DexWM without pretraining: 0% each.
results.interpretation: A physical transfer demonstration with a small sample, not a measured real-world reaching/placing result. No uncertainty interval is supplied.

results.task: RoboCasa image-goal reaching, placing and grasping
results.setting: 50 randomized trials per task after exploratory simulation adaptation; MPC execution.
results.comparison: Diffusion Policy: 16/8/0; DexWM without pretraining: 18/8/14, in the same task order. Human-pretrained DP separately reaches 4% average versus DexWM’s reported 53%.
results.interpretation: Reach requires mean hand-keypoint distance <15 cm; place object distance <10 cm; grasp wrist–object distance <20 cm plus contact, each sustained for ten steps. These criteria differ from physical secure-grasp judgment.

results.setting: Original EgoDex test split; all compared models trained on EgoDex for 40 epochs with DINOv2; 20 frames at 5 Hz over four seconds.
results.metric: PCK@20 (%) higher is better; embedding L2 error lower is better
results.value: DexWM PCK: 60 at four seconds / 68 average; L2: 0.67 / 0.51.
results.interpretation: DexWM improves average PCK by five percentage points over PEVA*, while PEVA* has lower feature error. The starred baselines are adaptations with restricted action conditioning, not unchanged original systems.

results.setting: Table 2 evaluates EgoDex rollouts, comparing HC disabled/enabled; PCK uses a 20-pixel tolerance.
results.value: With HC: PCK 60/69 and L2 0.66/0.50, at four seconds/average.
results.interpretation: The four-second gain is 34 percentage points, despite the prose calling it 34%. Table 2’s enabled row differs from the EgoDex-only row in Table 3; do not merge the configurations.

results.setting: Zero-shot open-loop evaluation on RoboCasa Lift sequences, before exploratory adaptation.
results.metric: Embedding L2 and PCK@20 at four seconds / average
results.interpretation: Human data improves cross-embodiment prediction, but absolute zero-shot hand accuracy remains low. Adding data changes both source diversity and training volume.

limitations.text: The model assumes deterministic, static scenes without external agents. Image goals are demonstrated; text goals and eliminating exploratory simulation adaptation remain future directions.

Table 6 attributes 70 percentage points of place trials to dropping the object, versus 72 total failure points. Grasp failures include 20 points of final-centimeter error and 18 of state drift. Strong hand localization does not establish reliable sustained contact.

The pretraining ablation removes both human and DROID pretraining, so Table 4 alone does not isolate human data. Qualitative counterfactuals are selected decoded predictions, without a controlled physical counterfactual accuracy benchmark.

reproduction.text: Required assets include DINOv2-L, annotated/calibrated EgoDex and DROID, exploratory RoboCasa trajectories, robot kinematics and the CEM initializer. Simulation planning is parallelized across eight H100 GPUs; reported planning time is 38–168 seconds per episode across tested settings, with 168 seconds the default. This is not a training-compute specification.

Clarify C.1’s eight-context-frame description versus target indices through i=9 before implementation. The supplied details leave the EgoDex 25-to-21-keypoint mapping, full grasp-orientation penalty, controller gains, software versions, seeds and training compute unspecified. Proposed checks should separate HC supervision from planning cost and test initialization dependence.

reasoning.text: The recorded Dual-system / Other mechanisms / Outside quadrants classification fits a forward world model coupled to external CEM and low-level control. Actions condition state prediction and are searched at inference; this is neither joint action/future generation nor inverse dynamics. Joint state/heatmap training does not make it an integrated action policy.

discussionQuestions: Does hand-consistency supervision improve contact prediction beyond image-space keypoint accuracy?
How much of grasp success depends on the dummy-grasp initializer?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title/author block and arXiv margin
evidence.detail: Exact catalog title; nine authors in catalog order; affiliations FAIR at Meta and New York University; arXiv:2512.13644v2 [cs.RO], 16 Mar 2026.

evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Section 1, problem motivation and dynamics definition
evidence.detail: Coarse action spaces and scarce dexterous robot data motivate human-video training; dynamics includes agent motion, environment response and camera appearance.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Figure 2 and Section 3 problem formulation
evidence.detail: Frozen image encoders supply latent histories to the action-conditioned predictor; its outputs feed the decoder and keypoint predictor.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section 3.1, Figure 3 and Eqs. (1)–(3)
evidence.detail: Each hand has 21 3D keypoints; keypoint differences are aligned to the earlier camera frame and supplemented by translation/Euler-angle changes. The action is 44 × 3. DROID uses dummy keypoints; Allegro repeats its last finger.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.2, Predictor and Multistep Prediction
evidence.detail: Deterministic CDiT with AdaLN conditioning directly regresses DINOv2 features. Future tokens start from the latest state; predicted states are fed back autoregressively.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.3, Eqs. (4)–(5) and training paragraph
evidence.detail: State MSE is supplemented by 12 heatmap MSE targets for wrists/fingertips, weighted by lambda=100, with the image encoder frozen.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 5–6, Section 3.4, Figure 4, Eq. (6) and Planning Cost
evidence.detail: CEM optimizes joint angles via forward kinematics and predicted terminal state. Cost combines latent L2 with keypoint-pixel distance weighted 0.001; grasping adds an orientation cost.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Table 1, RoboCasa columns and Section 4.2 Human Video
evidence.detail: DROID-only RoboCasa L2 is 1.3/0.96 and PCK 2/12; EgoDex+DROID yields 0.79/0.57 and 7/17, respectively at four seconds/average. Evaluation uses Lift.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Table 2, both HC rows and Section 4.2 Hand Consistency Loss
evidence.detail: HC off/on: four-second PCK 26/60, average 52/69; four-second L2 0.85/0.66, average 0.61/0.50. The prose describes the PCK change as 34%.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Table 3 and Sections 4.3–4.4; p. 8, Results
evidence.detail: Table 3 compares EgoDex-only training for 40 epochs using DINOv2, with four-second 20-frame rollouts and shared keypoint evaluation. DexWM PCK 60/68, L2 0.67/0.51; PEVA* 56/63, 0.62/0.49; NWM* 34/48, 0.74/0.57. Starred models restrict conditioning.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Section 4.5, Table 4 and surrounding training/evaluation/results paragraphs
evidence.detail: Table 4 reports simulation reach/place/grasp and physical grasp percentages: DP 16/8/0/0; no-pretraining DexWM 18/8/14/0; DexWM 72/28/58/83. Physical success is 10/12. Random-target versus Lift-initialized exploration gives 49% versus 53% average; human-pretrained DP gives 4%.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Figures 8–9 and comparison/controllability paragraphs; pp. 20–21, Figures 13–14
evidence.detail: Selected decoded rollouts compare text conditioning and structured hand actions. Atomic right-hand actions move 1 cm per frame; examples depict cup displacement on contact. These are qualitative predictions.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Section 5 Limitations
evidence.detail: Only image goals are demonstrated; approximately four hours of exploratory simulation remain necessary. Static scenes without external agents are assumed; stochastic extensions are future work.

evidence.location: PDF p. 15, Appendix A.1–A.4 and Table 5
evidence.detail: DINOv2-L uses 14-pixel patches, d=1024, 224 × 392 inputs and 448 patches. XL has 456M parameters, 32 blocks and 16 heads. The heatmap head has six transformer blocks and 2-pixel Gaussian targets. A ViT-L decoder is separately trained for visualization.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 15–16, Appendix B, Eq. (7), Figure 11 and implementation paragraphs
evidence.detail: CEM searches 23 joints. Simulation T/N/K/L=3/512/10/10 with replanning; real robot 2/256/10/10 without replanning. Controllers interpolate joints. Camera motion is excluded. Simulation uses eight H100 GPUs; tested planning times span 38–168 seconds, default 168. Grasp initialization uses a teleoperated dummy sequence.

evidence.location: PDF p. 16, Appendix C.1 Training Details
evidence.detail: Pretraining: Adam, batch 4096, 40 epochs, learning rate 1e-4 to 1e-7. Eight preceding frames are selected within four seconds, while target indices are stated as i=1,...,9. Fine-tuning: 50 epochs, batch 8, learning rate 1e-5, multistep prediction. Decoder training is separate.

evidence.location: PDF p. 17, Appendix C.2 and C.3
evidence.detail: EgoDex has 829 hours and 25 annotated keypoints per hand with approximately 1% held out; about 100 DROID hours are used. Exploratory data derives from noisy Lift actions plus gripper-only sequences. Only the right arm acts. Real evaluation uses four objects over 12 trials. NWM*/PEVA* are implemented within the authors’ framework.

evidence.location: PDF p. 18, Appendix C.3–C.5
evidence.detail: DP uses pooled DINOv2 observations, context two, action chunk nine and future-frame goals. Simulation reach/place thresholds are 15/10 cm; grasp requires wrist distance under 20 cm and contact, sustained for ten steps. Real grasp success is manually judged secure holding.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 18–19, Appendix C.6 and Table 6
evidence.detail: Failure percentages by contact/drop/last cm/state drift/total: reach 0/0/24/4/28; grasp 4/0/20/18/42; place 0/70/0/2/72. Text defines the four categories.

evidence.location: PDF p. 22, Figure 16 and caption
evidence.detail: Three physical grasp successes and one failure are illustrated. Green/red/blue borders identify start/goal/reached frames. The failure is an upside-down bowl displaced by gripper collision.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 6–7, Section 4.2, Figures 5–6 and encoder discussion
evidence.detail: Predictor scaling improves reported feature error and PCK. Encoder comparisons use simulation success because feature scales differ; dimensions are aligned by projections when needed. Performance varies by task.

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, abstract; p. 9, Table 4
evidence.detail: The abstract says over 50% average improvement over Diffusion Policy. Reader arithmetic from Table 4’s simulation rows gives mean success of 52.67% for DexWM and 8% for DP; the report uses task-specific values rather than interpreting the abstract phrase as a percentage-point gain.
